rungs.candidates: Peacock Gap Trail Run (San Rafael) -- REGISTERED, order 4496890
rungs.purpose: First race back — re-blood the racing instinct, milestone long run.
rungs.goal: Finish strong with a negative split. The clock is secondary — 2:15–2:45 is a realistic band on trail.
rungs.gate: One 15 mi long run (Block 2, week 21) and one full dress rehearsal at race effort.
rungs.fuel_target: 40-60 g carb/hr in the race, rehearsed at 65 g/hr in training
rungs.vert_prep: Peak training week ~4,000 ft; Peacock Gap runs the China Camp hills above San Rafael
rungs.teaches: Racing again after a long layoff, and that fuel goes in before you feel like you need it.
rungs.kit: Race shoes + handheld or light vest. Nothing unrehearsed.

rungs.candidates: A NorCal trail marathon. SPASM Lake Chabot (Castro Valley) runs a marathon alongside its 50K; Inside Trail and Coastal Trail Runs both card winter marathons.
rungs.purpose: The rung that makes the ladder legal. Without it the jump from half to 50K is 2.37x, past the ladder's own limit.
rungs.goal: Finish a marathon on trail without walking from exhaustion. Time is irrelevant — this race exists to make the 50K a small step instead of a leap. If this lands in late March, move the 50K to May/June: five weeks between a first marathon and a first 50K is not enough to recover and build.
rungs.gate: Longest run 18–20 mi, peak 30–33 mi/wk. You finish Block 2 at 33 mi/wk with a 15 mi long run, so this is a modest extension rather than a new build.
rungs.fuel_target: 50–70 g carb/hr for 4–5 hr — the first time fuelling matters more than fitness
rungs.vert_prep: 3,000–4,000 ft weeks; one long run with 2,000+ ft
rungs.teaches: What hours four and five feel like, and whether your stomach holds past the point where a half ends. Everything that breaks here is cheap to fix; the same failure in a 50K costs you the finish.
rungs.kit: Vest with 1L, the fuel you settled on at Peacock Gap, tested chafe strategy.
rungs.signup: Register Nov 21 – Dec 22 2026. That window opens two weeks BEFORE the Dec 5 half — book it while you are still training, not after.

rungs.candidates: SPASM Lake Chabot Trail Run (Castro Valley, ~Sat Apr 24) is the lead — it cards a 50K, marathon and 30K on one day. NOT Skyline 50K: despite being the classic first 50K, it runs early August, which leaves only 9 weeks to the October 50-miler.

rungs.signup: Register Dec 17 2026 – Jan 16 2027. Verify the date at the source first.
rungs.goal: Finish your first ultra. Walk the climbs on purpose, run the flats and downs. No bonk, no GI blowup.
rungs.gate: Longest run 20–22 mi, plus a back-to-back of 16 mi Sat / 10 mi Sun. Peak ~35–40 mi/wk, 4,000–5,000 ft/wk. The Feb marathon should have already covered most of this.
rungs.fuel_target: 60–80 g carb/hr, including real food (not gels alone) past hour 3
rungs.vert_prep: Sustained 4,000–5,000 ft weeks; single long runs with 2,000+ ft
rungs.teaches: Eating solid food while moving, and aid-station discipline — in and out, not a picnic.
rungs.kit: Vest with 1.5 L capacity, poles if the course is steep, tested chafe strategy.

mileage.rule: Build the long run ~1 mi every 1–2 wks. Weekly volume never grows more than 10% over the previous peak — the peak, not the cutback week, so a post-cutback rebound isn't a real jump. Every 4th week cut back ~30%.

week_structure.note: Legs-friendly around Strength A. Keep it easy.
Run before BJJ, or roll lighter that night. Your quality midweek run.
The most important run. Grows over time. Roll lighter Thu/Sat the week it jumps.

mileage.bjj_lever: BJJ is Mon / Thu / Sat, and the week already balances itself: Saturday is a teaching day, so the load is naturally light going into Sunday's long run. Thursday is the one day to roll hard -- nothing runs Thursday or Friday. Monday is the only real collision, sharing the day with the back-to-back run, so that is where intensity gives if something has to. Wednesday carries no BJJ at all, which leaves the quality run day clean.
mileage.ladder_note: 3 days carries you through the half and 50K. Add a 4th easy day in 2027 when 50-mile / 100 volume demands it.
mileage.vert_note: Weekly vertical gain is a tracked variable, not an afterthought: 1,600 ft in week 13 to 4,000 ft at peak. For the 100 it matters at least as much as mileage.
mileage.week_shape: Mon run + BJJ · Tue run + Strength A · Wed QUALITY run + mobility (no BJJ) · Thu BJJ (hard) + core · Fri Strength B · Sat teach · Sun LONG RUN

fueling.headline: Gut Training & Race Fueling
fueling.principle: The gut is trainable, and for anything past about three hours it is as likely to decide your race as your legs are. Carbohydrate tolerance goes up with deliberate, progressive practice — which means every long run is a nutrition session, not just a running session.
fueling.caveat: These are starting protocols built on general endurance-nutrition guidance, not a personalized prescription. Individual tolerance varies a lot. Log what you actually take and how your stomach actually felt, then adjust from your own data rather than from the table.

current_block.name: Trail Half Build
current_block.note: Ramps across 11 weeks. Week 21's peak long run (15 mi, Sun Nov 22) is the full dress rehearsal -- whatever works there becomes the Dec 5 race plan.

ladder.focus: Start fueling at 30 min. Establish that food goes in on a clock, not on hunger.
Introduce real food past hour 3. Gels alone stop working.
Sustain through a night section. Add a caffeine plan.
Document a fallback for when sweet stops working. Savory, broth, salt.
Desert sodium load, hot/cold food swaps, eating while sleep-deprived.

long_run_rules: Start fueling at 30 minutes. Every time. Not when you feel like it.
Fuel on a repeating timer, not on feel — the day you feel like eating is the day you're already behind.
Fluid 400–800 ml/hr, adjusted for heat and sweat rate. Sip steadily rather than gulping at aid.
Sodium 300–800 mg/hr, toward the top of that band in heat or if you finish crusted in salt.
Past 60 g/hr, split across two carb sources (e.g. glucose + fructose) — a single source hits an absorption ceiling.
Rehearse the race-day breakfast 2.5–3 hr before the peak long runs, not just the on-course fuel.
Log GI comfort 1–5 in the workout notes every long run. That log is the whole point.
Nothing new on race day. If it wasn't in a long run, it isn't in the race.

race_day_template.night_before: Normal-sized dinner, familiar food, nothing novel or high-fiber.
race_day_template.breakfast: 2.5–3 hr pre-start, the exact meal rehearsed in training. Carb-forward, low fibre, low fat.
race_day_template.final_top_up: ~15 min pre-start if the breakfast was early — small, liquid, familiar.
race_day_template.on_course: Begin at 30 min, then on a timer. Hit the block's g/hr target from the first hour.
race_day_template.when_it_goes_wrong: Back off the rate, switch to liquid calories or broth, slow down 10 minutes. Almost never fixes itself by pushing harder.
race_day_template.after: Refuel within 30–60 min: carbs + protein + fluid + sodium.

gi_troubleshooting.likely: Fluid ahead of absorption, or too concentrated a mix
gi_troubleshooting.try: Dilute the drink, slow the intake, keep moving easy until it clears.

gi_troubleshooting.symptom: Nausea late in a long effort
gi_troubleshooting.likely: Carb rate too high for current tolerance, or heat
gi_troubleshooting.try: Drop to liquid calories or broth, cool down, resume at a lower rate.
Have a savory option planned in advance — broth, salted potatoes, pretzels.

gi_troubleshooting.likely: Multifactorial — pace, sodium, and training load all play in
gi_troubleshooting.try: Ease the effort, take sodium, and note the conditions. Look for the pattern across several runs, not one.

fueling.products_to_test: Test at least two carb sources and one savory option in weeks 17-19, before they matter. Record brand, amount and GI comfort in the workout log.

trails.anchor: Anchored between San Mateo and Redwood City

They are not scenic picks — each one is chosen because its distance and climbing match what that specific week is trying to build. short_runs.headline: Short-Run Options
short_runs.principle: The Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday runs are three of your four running days, and they each want different ground — Monday flat, Tuesday gentle, Wednesday whatever that week's workout needs. Every session below gives you a Quick option near the house for days you're behind, a Trail option when you want dirt, and something New when the routine gets stale.
short_runs.rotation: Variety is the point, but not at the cost of the session. Rotate the Trail and New options week to week; keep the Quick one as the fallback that means the run still happens. A run done on the boring loop beats a run skipped because the good trail was an hour away.
short_runs.caveat: AllTrails figures. Trailhead distance is straight-line from the San Mateo / Redwood City midpoint, not drive time. Several of these are shared with mountain bikers — Water Dog and Big Canyon especially — so expect company on weekday evenings.

sessions.title: Back-to-back easy

sessions.avoid: Sustained climbing, technical footing, and any temptation to 'make it count'. Deliberately slow is the instruction.

options.why: 22 ft of gain across 4.5 mi — nothing else near you is this flat. Wide-open bay levee, a total change of scene from the redwoods.
options.how: Right distance as-is; cut it short anywhere.

sessions.need: Gentle rolling. Holding HR under the ceiling is the entire point of this run, and a steep climb spikes it — which quietly turns your easy day into a second hard day.
sessions.avoid: Anything you'd describe as a climb. If you're walking to keep HR down, the trail is wrong for this session, not you.

sessions.need: Undulating and runnable, so you can hold one steady comfortably-hard effort. Tempo means continuous — every steep pitch that forces a walk break breaks the session.
sessions.avoid: Real climbing. If you can't hold the effort through the terrain, it's a hill workout wearing a tempo costume.

sessions.avoid: Roots, rocks, ruts. Save the technical footing for a day you aren't sprinting.

coaching.headline: Running Coaching
coaching.principle: Three things decide whether a 48-year-old gets to a 100-mile start line intact: running easy enough on easy days, hiking climbs well rather than badly, and protecting the quads on descents. Everything below serves one of those three.
coaching.caveat: The heart-rate numbers are calculated from your resting HR of 56 and age 48 using standard formulas. Formula-based max HR carries roughly +/-10-12 bpm of individual variation, so treat these as a starting point, not a verdict. The talk test is the primary control; HR is the cross-check. If your heart rate behaves oddly against these bands -- and a documented thyroid condition is one reason it might -- trust the talk test and raise it with your doctor rather than forcing the numbers.

zones.basis: Resting HR 56, age 48. Max HR estimated 174 (Tanaka, 208 - 0.7 x age). Bands via Karvonen on a heart-rate reserve of 118. MAF (180 - age) independently gives 132, which sits inside the Zone 2 band below -- two different methods agreeing is why this ceiling is trustworthy enough to train on.
zones.talk_test: Zone 2 means full sentences without gasping. If you can only manage short phrases you are in Zone 3, which is the most common way endurance athletes ruin an easy day. If you can sing, you are too easy -- but that costs you far less than being too hard.
zones.ceiling: 140 bpm — the hard cap for every run labelled Easy. Walk the hills to stay under it.

bands.use: Monday back-to-back if the legs are hammered
Tuesday, Monday, and every long run. Most of your mileage lives here
Mostly a trap. Only for tempo work on Wednesdays

bands.feel: A few words at a time

bands.use: Hill repeat efforts only. Never on an easy day

skills.name: Power hiking — the ultra skill you don't have yet
skills.cue: Hands on quads, push down on each step. Short steps, tall chest, eyes 10 ft ahead. Drive with the arms.
skills.why: From the 50K up you will walk every steep climb, and hiking well is a trainable skill that is roughly as fast as running the same grade at a fraction of the cost. Most first-time ultrarunners lose more time hiking badly than they ever gain by running climbs.
skills.drill: On any climb over ~10% grade, hike it deliberately even when you could run. Practise on the Wednesday hill sessions and every Sunday climb.

skills.name: Downhill — what actually ends trail races
skills.cue: Quick light steps, let gravity do it, lean slightly INTO the hill not back. Never brake with a stiff leg.
skills.why: Braking on descents is eccentric quad loading, and that is the damage that shows up at hour six as legs that will not run any more. It is the single most under-trained skill in trail running.
skills.drill: The long descents at Huddart and Wunderlich are the training ground. Start conservative — downhill damage accumulates silently and you feel it two days later.

skills.name: Cadence
skills.cue: Aim ~170–180 steps/min. Count right-foot strikes for 30 s and double it, then double again.
skills.why: A low cadence means long strides, which means landing ahead of your body and braking on every step. Raising cadence is the cheapest form fix there is and reduces impact load per step.
skills.drill: If you are under 160, add 5% at a time, not all at once. A metronome app or 170+ bpm playlist works.

skills.name: Posture and lean
skills.cue: Tall through the chest, lean from the ANKLES not the waist. Head over shoulders over hips.
skills.why: Bending at the waist closes the diaphragm and cuts breathing efficiency exactly when you need it — which is why form collapses on climbs and late in long runs.
skills.drill: Every 10 minutes on a long run, run a check: head, shoulders, hips, hands. It takes three seconds.

skills.name: Arms and hands
skills.cue: Elbows ~90°, hands relaxed as if holding a crisp you don't want to crush. Swing front-to-back, not across.
skills.why: Clenched hands send tension up into the shoulders and neck, and cross-body arm swing rotates the torso and wastes energy over hours.
skills.drill: Every posture check, drop the shoulders and shake the hands out once.

skills.name: Foot strike and landing
skills.cue: Land under your hips, not out in front. Light and quiet — if you can hear yourself slapping, you're overstriding.
skills.why: Where you land matters far more than which part of the foot lands. Landing ahead of the body brakes; landing under it rolls you forward.
skills.drill: Fix it with cadence rather than by consciously changing your foot. Cadence corrects overstriding on its own.

skills.name: Eyes and line choice
skills.cue: Scan 10–15 ft ahead on trail, not at your feet. Pick the line before you get there.
skills.why: Looking straight down means reacting to every root instead of planning around it, and it drops your head, which drops your posture.
skills.drill: On technical ground at El Corte de Madera, deliberately lift the gaze. It feels wrong for a mile, then it feels obvious.

skills.name: Uphill running
skills.cue: Shorten the stride, keep the cadence, let the pace drop. Same effort, not same speed.
skills.why: Trying to hold pace uphill spikes HR into Z4 on what is supposed to be an easy run — the commonest way an easy day quietly becomes a hard one.
skills.drill: Watch HR on the Tuesday climbs. If it crosses 140, hike until it comes back down. That is the session working, not you failing.

warmup.before: 10 min easy jog, then 4 x 20 s strides building to fast-but-relaxed with a full walk-back. Required before Wednesday quality; optional before easy runs.
warmup.after: 5 min walk, then the mobility flow already in the plan. On long-run days get carbs and protein in within 30–60 min — that window matters more as you age.

stop_signals: Sharp pain — not soreness. Sharp means stop the run, today, no negotiation.
Pain that changes your gait. Limping to finish a session buys one workout and costs several weeks.
Resting HR up more than ~7 bpm from your 56 baseline for two mornings running — you are under-recovered or getting sick. Take the easy day, or take the day off.
HRV well below your ~42 ms weekly average alongside feeling flat. One low reading is noise; a trend is data.
Any chest symptom, unusual breathlessness, or your heart rate refusing to come down — stop and get it looked at. At 48, with a documented thyroid condition, that is not a run to push through.

recovery_sync.headline: Recovery Auto-Complete
recovery_sync.principle: Apple Health has no sensor for a sauna, a cold plunge or a red-light panel — nothing detects them. What it does record is a Mindfulness session, so one logged session can stand in for the whole stack you do alongside it. Everything the Watch can genuinely see is ticked automatically; everything it can't stays a manual tap.
recovery_sync.how_to_log: On the Watch: Mindfulness app → Breathe (or Reflect) for the length of your breathwork. That single session is what arrives here. You do not need to log the red light separately — the mapping below treats them as one morning block because that is how you actually do them.

signal.label: Mindful minutes
signal.note: Summed across every mindful session that day. Omitted entirely on days with none, so a missed day never overwrites a real value with a zero.

mappings.why: This IS the mindfulness session. A logged Breathe of 10 min or more is the breathwork.
Done in the same morning block as the breathwork, so the same session ticks it. Uncheck manually on days you skipped the panel.
No Health signal exists. Log it as an 'Other' workout if you want it counted later.
Would show as a Mind & Body workout if you started one, but it is usually done inside the mobility flow rather than logged separately.

recovery_sync.caveat: An auto-tick is evidence a session happened, not proof you did the whole stack. Untick anything you did not actually do — the log is only worth what it honestly records.

nutrition.headline: Nutrition Targets
nutrition.basis: Derived from your Function Health panel, not generic RDAs. Each target names the marker driving it. Synced daily from Apple Health, so whatever nutrition app you log in feeds this.
nutrition.medical_note: Several markers on your panel are substantially outside range — ApoB 175 (goal 70), LDL 199, triglycerides 321 (goal 80), LDL particle number 2761. Those are numbers a physician should be actively managing, not something to fix with a tracking dashboard alone. Treat everything here as support for a medical plan, not a substitute for one, and take this panel to your doctor if you have not already.

targets.name: Fiber
targets.why: Your highest-leverage food lever and the one you asked about. Soluble fibre binds bile acids and lowers LDL and ApoB directly; it also blunts glucose response and feeds the gut bacteria that keep CRP down. It is the single nutrient touching the most out-of-range markers you have.
targets.food: Oats, beans, lentils, chia, psyllium, berries, avocado. Build up gradually — jumping to 40 g overnight causes exactly the GI distress your gut training is trying to avoid.

targets.name: Sugar
targets.why: Triglycerides at 321 is the loudest number on your panel, and dietary sugar — fructose especially — is its most direct driver. Fructose also raises uric acid, which is separately above your goal.
targets.food: The cap is on added sugar, not fruit. Sports fuel during long runs is exempt: that carbohydrate is being burned, not stored, and the fuelling plan needs it.

targets.name: Saturated Fat
targets.marker: ApoB 175 · LDL 199 · Total cholesterol 297 · LDL small 509 · Pattern B
targets.why: Saturated fat raises LDL and ApoB more reliably than dietary cholesterol does. With ApoB at 2.5x your goal and a Pattern B particle profile, this is the fat lever that matters.
targets.food: Swap toward olive oil, nuts, avocado, fatty fish. Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated works better than just removing fat.

targets.name: Protein
targets.marker: Age 48 · 155 lb lean mass · 33 mi/wk peak training load
targets.why: About 1.6-1.8 g per kg of bodyweight. Protein needs rise with age and with endurance volume, and you are adding both. This protects lean mass through a block that is deliberately adding running and holding strength at maintenance.
targets.food: Spread across the day rather than one large serving. Aim for 30-40 g in the post-long-run window.

targets.name: Water
targets.why: Your own panel note says a BUN/Creatinine ratio of 30 is 'often hydration + protein load in heavy trainers'. You are raising protein AND mileage at the same time, which pushes it further in the wrong direction. This is the cheapest correction on the whole list.
targets.food: 120 fl oz is the BASELINE for a non-running day. Training adds on top — see the day-adjusted target on the chart. Front-load it: most of it before evening, or it costs you sleep.

dynamic.note: Baseline plus 20 fl oz per hour of running. Hours are estimated from the day's planned mileage at a 12 min/mi trail pace — deliberately rough, because the point is to drink more on big days, not to hit a decimal. Heat, or a day that leaves you crusted in salt, means more.

targets.name: Vitamin D
targets.why: Less than half your goal and flagged 'still low, keep supplementing'. Matters for bone density under rising running load, immune function, and hormone production.
targets.food: Diet alone rarely closes a gap this size — the supplement you are already taking is the main lever. This tracks what food adds on top.

targets.name: Folate
targets.why: Elevated homocysteine responds to folate, B12 and B6. Your panel note already says 'B-vitamins/methylation support'. Serum folate was not measured, so intake is the visible proxy.

targets.name: B12
targets.marker: Homocysteine 12.4 · B12 serum not measured (MMA 124, functionally in range)
targets.why: The functional marker looks fine, so this is maintenance rather than repair — tracked because it works with folate on the same homocysteine pathway.
targets.food: Animal protein covers this easily at your intake.

targets.name: Zinc
targets.why: Low-normal on the panel. Supports immune function and testosterone, both worth protecting through a heavy block.

targets.name: Magnesium
targets.why: Not a deficit; tracked because magnesium supports sleep quality and muscle function under load, and it is cheap to watch while you are logging anyway.
targets.food: Pumpkin seeds, dark chocolate, spinach, almonds.

targets.name: Potassium
targets.why: In range. Tracked for blood pressure and cramp management as long-run duration grows.

targets.name: Sodium
targets.why: Deliberately neutral rather than capped. Standard advice is to limit sodium, but you are about to sweat heavily for hours at a time and the fuelling plan calls for 300-800 mg per hour during long runs. Judge this against your training day, not a generic ceiling.
targets.food: Race and long-run intake is separate from daily baseline — do not confuse the two.

not_trackable.why: Your own panel note calls this 'the biggest easy win on the panel', and it is — three separate markers all point at it. But Apple Health has NO omega-3 identifier, so it cannot be charted here no matter which app you log in. It stays with your supplement stack and gets re-checked by blood test, not daily tracking.

nutrition.caveat: These are nutrition targets reasoned from your lab values using general clinical guidance. They are not a prescription, and I am not your physician. Numbers this far out of range — particularly the lipid panel — warrant a doctor's plan; use this to execute and track that plan, not to replace it.
